segments.translit: tam evā[rthaṃ] paramakaruṇāmreḍitasiddhācāryyo hi ḍombī| naukāpravāhavyājena prakaṭayati—
segments.translation: The [siddha]{siddha} master [Ḍombī]{p-dombi}, moved again and again by supreme compassion, makes that same point plain under the guise of a [boat]{boat} journey:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song as the work of the siddha master Ḍombī, who, moved again and again by supreme compassion, sets out ‘that same point’ under the guise of a boat journey. The phrase refers back to his preceding comment.

flags.note: paramakaruṇāmreḍita: āmreḍita literally means ‘repeated, reiterated’. I rendered ‘moved again and again by supreme compassion’; ‘steeped in’ supreme compassion is also possible. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) splits the compound: mchog gi snying rjes … slar yang, ‘by supreme compassion … again’, taking āmreḍita as ‘again’ (the siddha sets out the point once more). I kept the sense of the compound.

tam evārtham (‘that same point’) refers back to the comment on the previous song, which is outside this pack. Shastri's restoration [rthaṃ] is confirmed by the Tibetan de lta bu'i don, ‘such a meaning’.

naukāpravāhavyājena: the Tibetan has grus bsgrod pa dgongs pa'i skad kyis, ‘(spoke of) travelling by boat in the language of intention’. It renders vyāja ‘guise’ with dgongs pa'i skad, its phrase for sandhyābhāṣā in cp.14.m2, and pravāha as a journey (bsgrod pa). I changed ‘rowing a boat’ to ‘a boat journey’; pravāha can mean either. Because the glossary lists dgongs pa'i skad as a Tibetan form of sandhya-bhasa, a concordance will count this occurrence falsely.

The poet is named here simply ḍombī, without -pāda (the Tibetan has Dom+bi pa, with the personal suffix, so it too reads a name). I kept the surface ‘Ḍombī’ and linked it to p-dombi, whose approved English is ‘Ḍombīpāda’ (see questions).

segments.translit:
gaṅgetyādi| gaṅgāyamuneti sandhyayā candrābhāsasūryyābhāsau grāhyagrāhakau| yasyā[ḥ] śukranāḍikā viramānandāva[22ka]dhūtikāyā madhye varttate| sā eva nauḥ sandhyābhāṣayā boddhavyā|
sadguru ityādi vilakṣaṇaśuddhā| tatra sthitvā sahajayānapramattāṅgī ḍombī nairātmā saṃsārārṇave yogīndra[ḥ] pāraṃ karotīti|
segments.translation: ‘[Gaṅgā]{pl-ganga}’ and so on. The [Gaṅgā]{pl-ganga} and the [Yamunā]{pl-yamuna} are, in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}, the [moon]{moon}-[appearance]{abhasa} and the [sun]{surya}-[appearance]{abhasa}, [the grasped and the grasper]{grahya-grahaka}. The [avadhūtī]{avadhuti} of the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}, in the middle of which the channel of semen runs: that is what is to be understood, in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}, as the [boat]{boat}. ‘The true [guru]{guru}’ and so on: purified by [vilakṣaṇa]{vilaksana}. Staying there, [Ḍombī]{dombi}, [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, her body drunk with the vehicle of the [innate]{sahaja}, takes the [lord of yogis]{yogindra} [across]{para} the ocean of [saṃsāra]{samsara}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, in twilight language, as the moon- and sun-appearances, the grasped and the grasper. The boat is the avadhūtī (central channel) of the joy of cessation, where the channel of semen runs. Ḍombī, Nairātmā (selflessness as a goddess), drunk with the innate vehicle (the Tibetan: ‘drink’), ferries the lord of yogis across saṃsāra's ocean.

equations.en: the moon-appearance (candrābhāsa), the grasped; the pairing follows word order only
the sun-appearance (sūryābhāsa), the grasper; the pairing follows word order only
the avadhūtī of the joy of cessation, in the middle of which the channel of semen (śukranāḍikā) runs; the syntax also allows the channel itself
Nairātmā (in apposition, standing where the song has the Mātaṅgī; the Tibetan adds gdol pa'i bu mo, its word for the Mātaṅgī)

flags.note: yasyāḥ … viramānandāvadhūtikāyā madhye … sā eva nauḥ: I take the feminine relative yasyāḥ with avadhūtikāyāḥ, so that sā, the boat, is the avadhūtī of the joy of cessation within which the channel of semen runs. The syntax also lets sā pick up śukranāḍikā, which would make the channel of semen itself the boat, as the glossary's boat entry now reads it. The Tibetan (gang gis khu ba'i rtsa la … a wa d+hU tI'i dbus su 'jug pa'o / de'i phyir de nyid gru, ‘that by which the channel of semen enters the middle of the avadhūtī …; therefore that itself is the boat’) does not settle it. It has ‘enters’ ('jug pa) for vartate ‘lies, runs’.

sadguru ityādi vilakṣaṇaśuddhā is out of place: the refrain (sadguru …) is commented on in cp.14.m3, and what follows paraphrases line 1b (tahiṃ → tatra; pāra karei → pāraṃ karoti). The aligned Tibetan has nothing for the phrase: it passes straight from the boat to de la gnas pa'i (tatra sthitvā). That supports treating it as misplaced or intrusive in the Nepal manuscript. Translated as printed; the feminine vilakṣaṇaśuddhā would qualify the boat.

yogīndra[ḥ]: Shastri restores a nominative visarga, but the sense needs the accusative yogīndra[ṃ], and the Tibetan agrees: bdag med mas (agent) … rnal 'byor gyi dbang phyug pha rol du sgrol bar byed, ‘Nairātmā ferries the lord of yogis across’. I translated it as the object.

sahajayānapramattāṅgī ‘her body drunk with the vehicle of the innate’: the Tibetan has lhan cig skyes pa'i chang gi btung ba, ‘the drinking of the liquor of the innate’, reading -pāna- ‘drinking’ for -yāna- ‘vehicle’. pāna sits more naturally with pramatta ‘intoxicated’, and p and y are easily confused in manuscripts. The printed text makes sense, so I translated it as printed. I would support emending to sahajapāna- (‘drunk with drinking the innate’).
saṃsārārṇave ‘in the ocean of saṃsāra’: the Tibetan has 'khor ba'i gru la, ‘on the boat of saṃsāra’. Translated the Sanskrit.

For ḍombī nairātmā the Tibetan has gdol pa'i bu mo g.yung mo bdag med ma. gdol pa'i bu mo is its word for the song's Mātaṅgī (1b), and g.yung mo translates ḍombī (elsewhere the Tibetan transliterates Dom+bi, in the song and in the vocatives of cp.14.m3 and m5). So the Tibetan names the Mātaṅgī, Ḍombī and Nairātmā together, making explicit the identification that Munidatta's paraphrase implies. Its Sanskrit may have read mātaṅgī here.

In his paraphrase of 1b Munidatta puts Ḍombī, Nairātmā where the song has the Mātaṅgī girl, and supplies an object, the lord of yogis, which the line leaves unstated. tatra sthitvā ‘staying there’ answers tahiṃ buṛilī (draft ‘There … immersed’), and pramattāṅgī ‘drunk-bodied’ may answer poiālīle (draft ‘in play’). None of these is an explicit ‘X iti Y’ gloss. Of them I list only the apposition ḍombī = Nairātmā in equations.

viramānanda: the Tibetan renders it khyad par gyi dga' ba, ‘distinctive (special) joy’, here and in cp.14.m3. The name says nothing of cessation, as if the translators analysed vi-rama as ‘special delight’. I kept the glossary's ‘joy of cessation’, which follows the usual sense of virama (see questions).

Munidatta writes avadhūtikā; I used the approved English ‘avadhūtī’ (avadhuti). The Tibetan transliterates it (a wa d+hU tI) instead of using kun 'dar ma. It renders sandhyayā and sandhyābhāṣayā as dgongs pa'i skad, ‘language of intention’ (the sense sandhā); I kept the glossary's ‘twilight language’. candrābhāsasūryābhāsau is linked to moon, sun and abhasa; the Tibetan has one snang ba for both (zla ba dang nyi ma'i snang ba).

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena pratyayasandarśanāt| kulābhyāsaṃ kurute—
bāhutu ityādi| sahajaśodhitaviramānandanaumārge prāpte sati khānapānāśaktitvena bho ḍombi ātmānaṃ saṃbo[dhya] vadati kimarthaṃ vilamba[ḥ] kriyate| sadgurusaṃbodhyena nirantarābhyāsena punar jinapuraṃ mahāsukhapuraṃ atīva sannihitaṃ| evaṃ anucintyānudina[ṃ] pravāham abhyāsaṃ kuru|
segments.translation: By the [refrain]{dhruvapada}, because it shows grounds for confidence, he undertakes the practice of what is wholesome: ‘Row’ and so on. When the [boat]{boat}-path of the [joy of cessation]{viramananda}, purified by the [innate]{sahaja}, has been reached, he addresses himself, ‘O [Ḍombī]{dombi}’, and says: ‘Why is there this delay, through attachment to eating and drinking?’ Through the true [guru]{guru}'s teaching and unbroken practice, the [city of the Jina]{jinapura}, the city of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, is once again very near. Reflecting in this way, practise the rowing day after day.
segments.note: Munidatta hears the refrain as prompting wholesome practice. The singer tells himself: ‘O Ḍombī, why delay through attachment to eating and drinking?’ The boat-path of the joy of cessation, purified by the innate, is reached; through the true guru's teaching and unbroken practice the city of the Jina, the city of great bliss, is very near. So practise daily.

flags.note: kulābhyāsaṃ kurute: kula- is obscure here. The Tibetan has dge ba la goms par byed pa, ‘makes (one) practise virtue’, i.e. it read kuśalābhyāsa, ‘practice of the wholesome’; kula for kuśala is an easy haplography (ku[śa]la). Because the printed word is obscure, I translated with the Tibetan: ‘the practice of what is wholesome’. The alternatives I gave before (kula ‘family, lineage’; kūla ‘shore’; bahulābhyāsa ‘much practice’) now seem less likely. The subject of kurute is unstated.

pratyayasandarśanāt: I render ‘because it shows grounds for confidence’, taking pratyaya as ‘confidence’ and sandarśana as ‘showing’, since the refrain (the way is clear, the goal near) reads as encouragement. The Tibetan rkyen gyi yang dag par mthong ba las, ‘from seeing the conditions correctly’, takes pratyaya as ‘condition’ and sandarśana as ‘seeing’. Both are lexically possible.

khānapānāśaktitvena: the Tibetan zas dang skom la khyod chags sam, ‘are you attached to food and drink?’, confirms āsakti ‘attachment’ (not aśakti ‘inability’) and puts it inside the self-address, as the cause of the delay. I now construe it that way (‘Why is there this delay, through attachment to eating and drinking?’); before, I made it the reason he addresses himself. The Sanskrit allows both.

bho ḍombi ātmānaṃ saṃbodhya vadati: ‘he addresses himself, “O Ḍombī”, and says’. The Tibetan bdag nyid la 'bod par byed, ‘calls to himself’, confirms self-address rather than ‘rousing himself’. The poet is himself called Ḍombī, so Munidatta takes the refrain's vocative as the poet's self-address. This sits awkwardly with cp.14.m2 and m6, where Ḍombī is Nairātmā. The Tibetan transliterates the vocative (kye'i Dom+bi) as in the song, not g.yung mo as in m2, which is consistent with a name but not decisive. Linked to dombi to match draft 2a; p-dombi is arguable.

sadgurusaṃbodhyena: saṃbodhya is a gerundive or absolutive, not a noun; saṃbodhena (‘teaching, awakening’) is probably meant. Translated ‘the true guru's teaching’ (before: ‘instruction’, which the glossary reserves for upadeśa). The Tibetan has bla ma dam pa'i drin gyis, ‘by the kindness of the true guru’, as in its version of 2b (zhabs kyi drin gyis).

Smaller differences in the Tibetan: for naumārga ‘boat-path’ it has only lam ‘path’; for evaṃ anucintya ‘reflecting in this way’ it has de bzhin nyid kyi rjes su sems pas, ‘reflecting on suchness’, as if evam were tathatā; for anudinaṃ ‘day after day’ it has rgyun mi 'chad par ‘without interruption’. Translated the Sanskrit.

pravāham abhyāsaṃ kuru ‘practise the rowing’: pravāha here seems to render the song's bāha- ‘row’; it could also mean ‘practise in a steady stream’. The Tibetan has bsgrod cing goms par bya, ‘travel and practise’. The lemma bāhutu is the song's bāhatu.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadenābhyāsasyānuśaṃsām āhuḥ—
pañcetyādi| pañcakeṛuālam iti| pañcakramopadeśaṃ gṛhītvā kacchikāmaṇimūlaṃ gataṃ, tad eva bodhicittaṃ sahajānandena vivṛtaṃ sad vaimalyaṃ cakroddeśena pravāhaṃ kuru| gaganadukholakaṃ caturthābhiṣekeṇa sicyamānaṃ yogīndrasya kāye pānīyaṃ viṣayollolanaṃ viśati|
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} he speaks of the benefit of practice: ‘Five’ and so on. ‘Five [oars]{keruala}’: having taken up the [instruction]{upadesa} of the [five stages]{pancakrama}, make the rope—what has gone to the [root of the jewel]{manimula}, that very [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta}, opened by [innate joy]{sahajananda} and become stainless—flow toward the wheels. As the [sky]{gagana}-scoop is poured out through the fourth [empowerment]{abhiseka}, the water, the surging toward [sense objects]{visaya}, enters the body of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the five oars as taking up the five-stage instruction; the rope seems to be bodhicitta at the root of the jewel, to be made to flow toward the wheels. The sky-scoop is poured through the fourth empowerment. As printed, the water, the surging toward sense objects, enters the yogi's body; the Tibetan, like the song, says not.

equations.en: taking up the instruction of the five stages (pañcakramopadeśa)
what has gone to the root of the jewel (maṇimūla), that is, bodhicitta, on the Tibetan's word division; on Shastri's compound kacchikāmaṇimūla, the root of the jewel itself

flags.note: pānīyaṃ viṣayollolanaṃ viśati ‘the water … enters’: the song (3b) says the water does not get in (na paisai), and the Tibetan has the negative too: chu ni yul la g.yo ba mi 'jug pa'o, ‘the water, the stirring toward objects, does not enter’. With the song and the Tibetan agreeing, a na has very likely dropped out (viṣayollolanaṃ na viśati). Following the brief I translated the Sanskrit as printed and recorded the Tibetan in the note; I would support emending.

kacchikāmaṇimūlaṃ gataṃ: the Tibetan reads gdang bu ni nor bu'i rtsa bar gyur pa de nyid byang chub kyi sems, ‘the rope, which has reached the root of the jewel, is that very bodhicitta’; gdang bu is its word for the song's kācchī in 3a. I now follow this division, kacchikā | maṇimūlaṃ gataṃ (lemma, then gloss, as with pañcakeṛuālam iti), and translate kacchikā as ‘rope’ with the draft. Shastri prints one compound, which gives ‘what has gone to the rope, the root of the jewel’ and makes the rope the root of the jewel itself (my previous version).

vivṛtaṃ ‘opened’ (by innate joy): the Tibetan has rnam par bzung, ‘held’, as if reading vidhṛtaṃ. ‘Held’ suits the retention of bodhicitta and the song's rope that is tied. The printed word makes sense, so I translated it as printed.

cakroddeśena pravāhaṃ kuru: the Tibetan has 'khor lo'i phyogs su 'bab par bya'o, ‘make it flow toward the wheel’. I changed ‘row by way of the wheels’ to ‘make … flow toward the wheels’: uddeśa can mean ‘direction’, and with bodhicitta as the object pravāha reads as ‘flowing’ (in cp.14.m3 it glosses the song's rowing). The wheels are those of the subtle body, so not linked to the glossary's ‘wheel’, the image of 4a; the Tibetan's singular may mean one wheel.

gaganadukholakaṃ … sicyamānaṃ has no finite verb; I take it as an absolute clause (‘as the sky-scoop is poured out’). The Tibetan takes the sky-scoop as a lemma (nam mkha'i ko ba ni) and attaches the empowerment to the yogi (dbang bzhi pas dbang bskur ba dang ldan pa'i rnal 'byor gyi dbang phyug, ‘the lord of yogis empowered by the fourth empowerment’), which the neuter sicyamānaṃ does not strictly allow.
viṣayollolana: the Tibetan yul la g.yo ba, ‘stirring toward objects’, takes the compound as locative. I changed ‘the surging of sense objects’ to ‘the surging toward sense objects’.

sad vaimalyaṃ: vaimalya is a noun (‘stainlessness’); I read it as if vimalaṃ, ‘become stainless’. The Tibetan dri ma med pa brgya yis, ‘by a hundred stainless …’, seems to read śata ‘hundred’ for sad, and does not help.

For pañcakeṛuāla the Tibetan has skya ba 'dzin pa, ‘oar-holders’, as in its version of 3a. It renders anuśaṃsā literally as rjes su bsngags pa, ‘praise’ (also in cp.14.m6); I kept ‘benefit’, the usual Buddhist Sanskrit sense. It counts the verses as Munidatta does (rkang pa gnyis pa, gsum pa, bzhi pa), leaving out the refrain.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadenābhyāsaviśeṣād ābhāṣa[23]trayanirodham āhu[ḥ]—
cāndetyādi| candraṃ prajñājñānaṃ sūryyam utpādād advayajñānaṃ pulindaṃ sandhyābhāṣayā napuṃsakaṃ| traya ete saṃsārasya sṛṣṭisaṃhārakārakāḥ| sarvvadharmmānupalambhajaladhau gacchan san vāmadakṣiṇam agrapaścāt tīram anupaśyantīti bho ḍombi svacchandena vilakṣaṇaśodhitaṣodhicittanauvāhanābhyāsaṃ kuru|
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he speaks of stopping the three [appearances]{abhasa} through a special practice: ‘[Moon]{moon}’ and so on. The [moon]{moon} is the knowledge of wisdom; the [sun]{surya}, from arising; nondual knowledge, the [pulinda]{pulinda}, is in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa} the neuter. These three bring about the [creation and destruction]{srsti-samhara} of [saṃsāra]{samsara}. Going on the ocean where no phenomenon is apprehended, they look to the shore left and right, ahead and behind. O [Ḍombī]{dombi}, as you please, practise rowing the [boat]{boat} of [bodhicitta]{bodhicitta} purified by [vilakṣaṇa]{vilaksana}.
segments.note: Munidatta says a special practice stops the three appearances. The moon is the knowledge of wisdom, the pulinda in twilight language ‘the neuter’ (the sun's gloss is corrupt). These three make and unmake saṃsāra. As printed, travellers look to the shore; the Tibetan, like the song, says not. Ḍombī should freely row the boat of bodhicitta purified by vilakṣaṇa.

equations.en: unclear as printed: ‘from arising’ (utpādāt); perhaps originally the knowledge of means (upāyajñāna)
in twilight language, the neuter (napuṃsaka); probably also nondual knowledge (advayajñāna)
bodhicitta purified by vilakṣaṇa (‘the boat of bodhicitta’)

flags.note: sūryam utpādād advayajñānaṃ: the gloss on the sun is incomplete or corrupt. The pairing with prajñājñāna leads one to expect upāyajñānam (‘the knowledge of means’). I translated literally (‘the sun, from arising’) and took advayajñānam (‘nondual knowledge’) with the pulinda, which suits the neuter as a third term uniting the two. It could instead belong to the sun (‘the sun, from arising, is nondual knowledge’).

The aligned Tibetan has nothing for the lemma cāndetyādi, the glosses of the moon, the sun and the pulinda, or traya ete. It passes from the opening sentence to 'khor ba skyed pa dang sdud pa'i byed pa po'o, ‘(they) are the agents of the creation and withdrawal of saṃsāra’. So it cannot help with the corrupt gloss on the sun, and the readings the glossary takes from this segment (moon, pulinda) rest on the Sanskrit alone. Whether the gap is in the Tengyur or in the alignment should be checked.

tīram anupaśyantīti ‘they look to the shore’: the song (4b) says ‘not looking’ (na rebai), and the Tibetan has the negative: g.yas g.yon dang mdun rgyab tu mi lta ba, ‘not looking right and left, ahead and behind’ (with no word for ‘shore’). With the song and the Tibetan agreeing, a lost na is likely (tīraṃ nānupaśyanti). Translated as printed and recorded in the note. The subject is also unclear: gacchan san is masculine singular, anupaśyanti plural.
ṣodhicitta is a misprint or miscopying for bodhicitta (ষ for ব); the Tibetan has byang chub kyi sems. Translated as bodhicitta.

ābhāṣa is ābhāsa, ‘appearance’ (the abhasa entry); the Tibetan snang ba gsum, ‘three appearances’, confirms it. For vilakṣaṇaśodhita the Tibetan has mtshan nyid dang bral bas rnam par sbyangs pa, ‘purified by freedom from characteristics’, the etymological rendering, which favours the technical term over ‘extraordinarily purified’.

vilakṣaṇaśodhitabodhicittanauvāhanābhyāsaṃ kuru ‘practise rowing the boat of bodhicitta purified by vilakṣaṇa’: the Tibetan has byang chub kyi sems kyis gru la goms par bya, ‘with bodhicitta, practise on the boat’, which makes bodhicitta the means rather than the boat and drops ‘rowing’. Translated the Sanskrit compound.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena nairātmadharmmasya phalānuśaṃsām āhu[ḥ]—
kabaḍītyādi| yathā bāhye pārāvāre tarapatis tarakaparddikāṃ gṛhṇāti| tadvad grāhyagrāhakatayā sā bhagavatī ḍombī nairātmā na pratigṛhṇāti| artha paricaryyāmātreṇāgrāhyatayā bhavasamudre pāraṃ karotīti| nairātnadharmmāparicayena bahiḥśāstrābhimānino ye yoginas te 'pi kule śarīre bhramantīti ajñānenāvṛtā bālā ityādi| 14||
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he speaks of the benefit that the teaching of [selflessness]{nairatmya} yields as its fruit: ‘[Cowrie]{kabadi}’ and so on. Just as in the outer world the ferry-master at a crossing takes a [cowrie]{kabadi} as the fare, the blessed lady [Ḍombī]{dombi}, [Nairātmā]{nairatma}, does not accept in that way, in the manner of [the grasped and the grasper]{grahya-grahaka}. Rather, with service alone, being beyond grasping, she ferries [across]{para} the ocean of becoming. Those [yogis]{yogi} who, unacquainted with the teaching of [selflessness]{nairatmya}, pride themselves on outer treatises: they too wander on the [shore]{kula-shore}, that is, in the body. ‘Fools veiled by ignorance…’ and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta contrasts the ordinary ferry-master, who takes a cowrie as fare, with the blessed Ḍombī, Nairātmā, who accepts nothing as grasped and grasper and ferries across the ocean of becoming for mere service (the Tibetan suggests ‘mere acquaintance’). The shore he reads as the body, where yogis proud of outer treatises, unfamiliar with selflessness, wander.

citations.quoted: ajñānenāvṛtā bālā ityādi (‘Fools veiled by ignorance…’ and so on)
citations.work: unidentified; Munidatta names no source, and the Tibetan renders the words as a sentence of the comment, not as a quotation

flags.note: artha paricaryāmātreṇa: artha makes no sense as printed; probably atha (‘rather, but’) or arthāt (‘that is to say’). Translated ‘Rather’. If paricaya is read (next flag), artha may belong in the compound: arthaparicayamātreṇa, ‘by mere acquaintance with the meaning’.

paricaryāmātreṇāgrāhyatayā ‘with service alone, being beyond grasping’: the Tibetan has shes ba (read shes pa) tsam du bzung ba de yis, ‘by holding (it) as mere knowing’. That points to paricaya ‘acquaintance, familiarity’ rather than paricaryā ‘service’. The next sentence uses paricaya in the negative (aparicaya, Tibetan 'dris med pa ‘unfamiliar’): she ferries across those merely acquainted, while yogis unacquainted with the teaching wander. The Tibetan also lacks the negative of agrāhyatayā. The printed text makes sense, so I translated it as printed.

nairātmadharma: the Tibetan distinguishes the two occurrences. The first is bdag med pa'i chos, ‘the dharma of selflessness’, the second bdag med ma'i chos, ‘the dharma of Nairātmā’. The Sanskrit allows both (nairātma- can be the shortened feminine stem in compound). I linked both to nairatmya (selflessness); the second could read ‘unacquainted with Nairātmā's teaching’. The glossary lists the form under nairatma.

For tadvad the Tibetan has de kho na nyid la, ‘in reality’, and for sā bhagavatī ḍombī nairātmā only bcom ldan 'das ma bdag med ma, without ḍombī. Its ‘in reality she does not take’ supports my reading of tadvad … na pratigṛhṇāti as a contrast (‘does not accept in that way’) rather than ‘likewise does not accept’.

For tarakaparddikā ‘a cowrie as the fare’ the Tibetan has glu dbyangs 'gron bu la sogs pa, ‘songs, cowries and so on’, perhaps misreading tara-. For kule śarīre it has lus kyi ngogs su, ‘on the bank of the body’, which confirms kula as kūla ‘shore’. It renders ajñānenāvṛtā bālā ityādi not as a quotation but as a sentence echoing 5b: mi shes pa'i byis pa rnams ngogs su 'bying bar 'gyur ro, ‘the ignorant fools sink at the bank’.

Munidatta does not explicitly gloss ‘those who climbed onto a chariot’ (5b); in his paraphrase the yogis proud of outer treatises stand in their place. paricaryā (‘service’) is not the glossary's caryā (‘conduct’), despite the automatic hit, and is not linked; nor is bhagavatī linked to bhaga or to p-bhagavat.
nairātna- is a misprint for nairātma-.
The closing ‘14||’ is the song number, not Munidatta's wording, and is not translated.

questions: Negations (cp.14.m4, m5): the Tibetan (Toh 2293) has the negatives the printed Sanskrit lacks (mi 'jug, ‘does not enter’; mi lta ba, ‘not looking’), agreeing with the song (3b, 4b). Following the brief I translated the Sanskrit as printed and put the Tibetan in the flags and notes. Should the translation be emended to ‘does not enter’ and ‘do not look’, with a flag?

Tibetan readings I recorded but did not adopt, because the printed Sanskrit makes sense: -pāna- ‘drinking’ for -yāna- ‘vehicle’ (m2), vidhṛtaṃ ‘held’ for vivṛtaṃ ‘opened’ (m4), paricaya ‘acquaintance’ for paricaryā ‘service’ (m6). Adopt any of them? The one Tibetan reading I did adopt is kuśala for the obscure kula- in m3 (‘the practice of what is wholesome’). Please confirm that.

cp.14.m4: I now follow the Tibetan's word division (kacchikā | maṇimūlaṃ gataṃ), so the rope is bodhicitta that has reached the root of the jewel, rather than Shastri's compound (the rope is the root of the jewel). Accept? If so, the manimula definition (‘rowed by way of the wheels’) should change to match ‘made to flow toward the wheels’, and kācchī may deserve its own entry carrying this reading.

cp.14.m2: the aligned Tibetan lacks ‘sadguru ityādi vilakṣaṇaśuddhā’. Keep it in the translation as printed (as now), or mark it as probably intrusive? The vilaksana definition cites this passage; on the Tibetan evidence cp.14.m5 is its secure attestation.
cp.14.m5: the aligned Tibetan lacks the glosses on the moon, sun and pulinda. Can the Tengyur folio be checked, to see whether the gap is in the text or in the alignment?
viramānanda is rendered khyad par gyi dga' ba, ‘distinctive joy’, in the Tibetan (m2, m3). Keep ‘joy of cessation’? Should the viramananda entry mention this rendering?

p-dombi: in cp.14.m1 the poet is called only ḍombī (Tibetan Dom+bi pa). I linked the surface ‘Ḍombī’ to p-dombi (approved English ‘Ḍombīpāda’). Should the entry list ‘Ḍombī’ as a variant, or should the commentary read ‘Ḍombīpāda’?

cp.14.m3: Munidatta takes the refrain's ‘O Ḍombī’ as the poet addressing himself (the Tibetan confirms: bdag nyid la 'bod pa). Link it to p-dombi or to dombi (I used dombi)? And should the dombi entry record this reading beside the Nairātmā one?

boat entry: the grammar of cp.14.m2 (yasyāḥ … avadhūtikāyāḥ … sā) favours the avadhūtī of the joy of cessation as the boat, with the channel of semen inside it; the Tibetan does not settle it. The entry currently says the channel. Revise?

matangi entry says its reading is unattested. In cp.14.m2 Munidatta's paraphrase of 1b puts ‘Ḍombī, Nairātmā’ where the song has the Mātaṅgī, and the Tibetan of that passage names her outright (gdol pa'i bu mo, its word for the Mātaṅgī in 1b, beside g.yung mo and bdag med ma). Record this as a reading, attributed to the paraphrase and noting the Tibetan?

nairātmadharma (cp.14.m6) is listed as a form of nairatma. The Tibetan reads the first occurrence as selflessness (bdag med pa'i chos) and the second as Nairātmā's (bdag med ma'i chos). I linked both to nairatmya. Split them, and move the form?

False glossary matches, not linked: carya in paricaryā (m6), citta inside bodhicitta and ṣodhicitta (m4, m5), bhaga inside bhagavatī (m6). Also the sandhya-bhasa Tibetan form dgongs pa'i skad renders vyāja ‘guise’ in m1.
The words ‘ajñānenāvṛtā bālāḥ …’ (cp.14.m6) are unidentified, and the Tibetan renders them as a sentence (‘the ignorant fools sink at the bank’), not as a quotation. Can you trace them?
